scene1: Getting a design system from Figma into code usually has a hand-off in the middle: export the tokens, wire them in, rebuild the components, check them by eye.
This skill is one door instead.
It reads Figma directly, generates tokens, Foundations pages and components in Storybook, and proves that what it built matches Figma.
scene2: Figma Desktop runs a plugin, the Desktop Bridge.
Through the figma-console MCP the AI can run JavaScript inside the Figma file.
Anything big is written straight to disk by a small local server, bundled scripts turn those files into code, and a last stage checks the result against Figma.
scene3: A tiny local server on port 9232.
The plugin posts big reads to it and they land as files, so they never pass through the AI's context.
It also serves the plugin scripts.
Plugin scripts used to be pasted into every call, about 4 KB each.
Now the call fetches the script from the server and passes ARGS, the parameters. About 280 bytes.
We read variables, scopes and styles from Figma ourselves and write them in the Tokens Brücke shape.
Anything that already consumes a Brücke export keeps working, with nobody exporting anything.
buildTokens turns that file into CSS variables, a Tailwind 3 theme and the typo-* text-style classes; buildTokenDocs writes the Foundations pages.
Four more pieces round it out: inventory, the component analysis, initStorybook and checkConfig.
scene4: The index is the map back into Figma.
Every one of the 714 variables has its Figma ID next to its CSS variable, its classes and its values; so do the 58 text styles and 23 effects.
Each built component has a pointer too: the Button is node 7:21282, on the Button page, 360 variants.
When the design changes, the skill does not scan the file.
It checks that the IDs still resolve, then reads exactly that node.
We tested it: reading the Button by its ID returned the same file as reading it by name, and a made-up ID was reported missing right away.
scene5: What comes out of the foundation step: Graphene's 903 variables in 10 collections become 714 CSS variables, with Dark as a data-theme override.
The colour palette and semantic tokens, the text styles, spacing and sizing, radius and borders, and the effects: six Foundations pages, generated, not written by hand.
scene6: The Button is 360 variants in Figma.
In code it is one component.
Kind, status and size become props; hover and press are CSS states.
Twenty-four combinations of kind and status, side by side.
Then five checks: the side-by-side sheet, hover and press values against the token, disabled and loading values, every class resolving to CSS, and every story rendering.
Statuses, sizes, disabled and read-only all match Figma, with the label, info icon and caption.
A fresh agent built it using only the skill.
scene8: All the big data now goes to disk.
The first test of the skill, building Input with a fresh agent, used about 184 thousand tokens.
Most of it came from reading a 775-line analysis output, pasting the same 5 KB script again and again, and the agent writing its own browser helper.
Those gaps are closed in the skill.
scene9: A project with no Storybook: the skill detects the stack and adds only what is missing; it never overwrites your files.
We ran it on the MVP before it had Storybook, on rsbuild and on Vite.
A project that already has Storybook: update tokens or one component.
And an empty folder: a starter template, then the same flow.
scene10: Today it supports React 18 with Tailwind 3.
Tailwind 4, projects without Tailwind, and Next.js are not supported yet: the skill stops and says why, because the workflow differs there and there is no template.
Webpack, and Dark mode in the component comparison, are not tested yet.
Next: the other stacks, and more components through the same pipeline.
